quote: vermuthe ich den allgemeinen Satz: Kommt in der Differentialgl. ein Parameter $\lambda$ linear vor z.B. $\Delta u + \lambda u^2 = 0$, so ist das durch die Randbedingungen bestimmte Integral $u$ in $\lambda$ vom Charakter einer algebraischen Funktion d.h. [-hat nur eine-] $u$ ist in $\lambda$ analytisch und hat nur einzelne algebraische Singularitäten.
english: I conjecture the general theorem: if a parameter λ occurs linearly in the differential equation, e.g. Δu + λu² = 0, then the integral u determined by the boundary conditions has, as a function of λ, the character of an algebraic function, i.e. u is analytic in λ and has only isolated algebraic singularities.
topic: Notes on how to determine general integrals of partial differential equations by boundary data on non-characteristic curves, a conjecture that such solutions depend algebraically on a linearly occurring parameter, and a claim about closed geodesics on closed surfaces illustrated by Finsterwalder's lamella model.

triage.modern_statement: Take a nonlinear elliptic boundary value problem in which a real or complex parameter λ appears linearly, for example Δu + λu² = 0 in a domain Ω with fixed (say Dirichlet) boundary data, written abstractly as F(λ,u) = A(u) + λB(u) = 0 between Banach spaces, with F analytic and Fredholm. The question is whether the solution u(λ) singled out by the boundary conditions behaves like a branch of an algebraic function of λ. That would mean u extends analytically in λ, and its only singularities are isolated branch points with Puiseux-type (fractional power) expansions, such as folds or bifurcation points, rather than essential or non-isolated singularities. In modern terms this is a question about the analytic structure of solution sets of parameter-dependent nonlinear operator equations, i.e. analytic bifurcation theory.
triage.answered_by: The local version was settled in Hilbert's own Göttingen circle. Erhard Schmidt was Hilbert's doctoral student; his 1906 Bonn Habilitationsschrift was published as 'Zur Theorie der linearen und nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen III: Über die Auflösung der nichtlinearen Integralgleichung und die Verzweigung ihrer Lösungen', Math. Ann. 65 (1908) 370–399. Together with Lyapunov's work, it created the Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction. This reduction turns an analytic Fredholm problem near a singular parameter value into a finite-dimensional analytic 'branching equation'. Solving that equation by Puiseux series gives exactly the 'analytic with isolated algebraic branch points' behaviour, though only locally. The global theory for real-analytic one-parameter families came from E. N. Dancer (1970s) and was developed by B. Buffoni and J. Toland in 'Analytic Theory of Global Bifurcation' (Princeton, 2003). It shows that solution sets contain globally defined continuous curves that can be reparametrized real-analytically around each point. The conjecture as Hilbert phrased it (a global 'algebraic function' character) is not stated or proved in this form in any source I found. Global solution branches may run off to infinity or lose compactness, which is why the modern theorems include alternatives for this; I found no explicit counterexample in the sources.

evidence.claim: E. Schmidt, 'Zur Theorie der linearen und nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen III. Über die Auflösung der nichtlinearen Integralgleichung und die Verzweigung ihrer Lösungen', Math. Ann. 65, 370–399 (1908): an early treatment of how solutions of nonlinear integral equations branch as a parameter varies.
This paper began as Schmidt's Habilitationsschrift (Univ. Bonn, 1906), following his Göttingen dissertation (1905).

The Lyapunov–Schmidt methods underlie the bifurcation theory of parameter-dependent functional equations, going back to Lyapunov, Poincaré and E. Schmidt, and the area still has active special issues.
Later work (Melamed, 1971) on branching of solutions of nonlinear equations with complex parameters builds on Schmidt's paper.

Dancer's global bifurcation theory for real-analytic one-parameter families gives globally defined continuous curves of solutions that are locally real-analytic. This is a much stronger notion of parameter dependence than topological (Rabinowitz) theory gives.
The Dancer/Buffoni–Toland analytic global bifurcation theorem is used today, e.g. for water waves: it gives a solution curve with a real-analytic parametrization locally around each of its points.
Recent work (2025) still applies and refines the analytic global bifurcation theorem for real-analytic Fredholm maps.

triage.why: The note is a real research question: how solutions of nonlinear boundary value problems depend analytically on a parameter. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Schmidt's 1908 branching theory, written by Hilbert's student in this very period, answers the local form: for analytic Fredholm problems, solutions are analytic in λ except at isolated branch points, where Puiseux expansions apply. Dancer and Buffoni–Toland's analytic global bifurcation theory gives the modern global picture. That picture is real-analytic curves with possible loss of compactness or blow-up, not a literally 'algebraic function' character. That is why I call it 'solved' in modern form rather than 'open', but with low confidence. None of the sources I found link Hilbert's notebook entry directly to Schmidt or to Dancer, so the connection is my own reading of the mathematics, not a documented historical line. The global claim exactly as Hilbert worded it does not appear verbatim as a theorem in these sources. Analytic bifurcation theory is still an active area, for example in water waves.
